proposals.butler: Neptune, however, lay with his daughter
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, high) on 'Poseidon, however, lay with his daughter': "'his' = Eurymedon's ... On first pass 'his' reads as Poseidon's own daughter" (noted as a first-pass misread). book_level repeats it: "'Poseidon, however, lay with his daughter' first reads as Poseidon's own daughter".
proposals.reason: A new paragraph opens with Poseidon as subject, so English takes 'his daughter' as his own. The default parse has Poseidon lying with his own daughter and garbles the genealogy that is the point of Athena's speech; the reader recovered only by going back to ¶5. Butler's referent is certain (Homer, Od. 7.61, has 'with her'): Periboea, 'the youngest daughter of Eurymedon', named in the sentence before. Naming the father keeps Butler's 'daughter' and asserts nothing new. It is the same pronoun-to-antecedent repair the 2026-09-23 screening made in this paragraph ('But Rhexenor left a daughter').
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶6: Neptune, daughter, son, Nausithous, Phaeacians, Rhexenor, Alcinous, Apollo, bridegroom, male issue, Arete, honours, keep house, husbands. 'Eurymedon' does not occur in ¶6 (Butler names him in ¶5, the antecedent). No Butler word is reused for anything else.

proposals.butler: you may have every hope of seeing your friends again
proposals.reader_evidence: The Book's one 'misread' (medium) is on 'seeing your friends again': "Seeing his own people, family and loved ones again; a modern reader takes 'friends' literally". Note: older usage of 'friends' = kin; 'recurs in ¶12'. book_level: the Book 'never shows that Odysseus longs for his family, so his motives read as more material than they are probably meant to be.'
proposals.reason: Butler's 'friends' carries the Victorian sense of one's own people, kin (Greek philous, Od. 7.76: 'to see your dear ones and reach your high-roofed house'). Present-day 'friends' excludes family. A typical reader narrows the promise to friends and, with 7.18's 'property ... bondservants ... house', misreads what Odysseus longs for. 'Loved ones' is the current word for the same circle. Earlier in this paragraph Butler's 'when any women are friends of hers' is the current sense and stays, so the paragraph now renders one Butler word two ways by sense. That is a deliberate discrimination to record, like 'raiment' → robes/clothing (Book 8 continuity §6).
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶7: respected, children, Alcinous, the whole people, goddess, greet, city, good woman, head and heart, women, friends (of hers), husbands, disputes, good will, hope, friends, home and country. 'Loved' and 'ones' do not occur. 'Your own people' was rejected: Butler's 'the whole people' (the Phaeacian populace) is in this paragraph, and 'people' is his word for the populace throughout Book 7.

proposals.butler: for I have been long in trouble and away from my friends
proposals.reader_evidence: Flagged in ¶7's misread barrier ('recurs in ¶12') and in book_level: "'Friends' (¶7, ¶12) seems to mean family or his own people". The reader's own ¶12 paraphrase has to supply 'far from his own people'.
proposals.reason: The same kin sense as 7.7 (Greek philon apo, Od. 7.152: 'far from my dear ones'), in Odysseus's first plea to the queen. Read as 'friends', it drops the family he is trying to reach. The rendering matches B07-02, per the consistency rule.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶12: Queen Arete, daughter, Rhexenor, distress, humbly pray, husband, guests, heaven, prosper, long life, happiness, possessions, children, honours, state, help me home, own country, trouble, friends. 'Loved' and 'ones' do not occur.

proposals.quote_modern: they have made themselves perfectly clear to us
proposals.replacement: they have made themselves perfectly manifest to us
proposals.butler: for hitherto they have made themselves perfectly clear to us when we have been offering them hecatombs
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, medium) on 'they have made themselves perfectly clear to us': "The gods have always appeared openly, in visible form; not the modern idiom 'explained themselves clearly'." On the next sentence the reader adds: 'the link to his invisible arrival is left for the reader to make.'
proposals.reason: Butler's 'clear' means clearly seen: the Greek has the gods appearing 'in manifest form' (enargeis, Od. 7.201). In current English 'make oneself perfectly clear' is a fixed idiom for unambiguous speech. A typical reader therefore takes the gods to have always 'been clear' with the Phaeacians, and the ground of Alcinous's argument is lost: a god arriving hidden would be unusual because the gods come to them openly and undisguised. One word changes. 'Manifest' (appearing in visible form) is the exact sense, keeps Butler's construction and his 'perfectly', and suits his register.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶17: aldermen, councillors, words, supper, bed, to-morrow, banquet, honour, guest, escort, rejoicing, country, trouble, inconvenience, distant, harm, homeward journey, luck, immortals, heaven, usual practice, hitherto, clear, hecatombs, feasts, wayfarer, stumble, affect no concealment, near of kin, Cyclopes, giants. 'Manifest' occurs nowhere in Butler's Book 7. Alternatives rejected: 'visible' is plainest but is Butler's own word at 7.11 ('he became visible'), so one rendering would serve two Butler words (arrow B); the lead may prefer it if that echo is judged harmless. 'Plain(ly)' is Butler's 'plainly' in the 7.13 formula, and 'shown' is Butler's 'show' at 7.2, 7.3 and 7.5.

rejected_barriers.quote: So Odysseus waited and prayed
rejected_barriers.reason: Carried over from Book 6 (assignment note). The sentence states what he does; not a wording defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: the girl
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's own design: she is Book 6's Nausicaa and is named at the end of this paragraph. The reader identified her correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: carried the clothes into the house
rejected_barriers.reason: The washing trip belongs to Book 6. Butler's sentence; the reader's reading (laundry) is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: had been chosen as a prize for Alcinous
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader's reading (a captive picked out as the king's special share) is exactly Butler's sense (Greek geras, a prize of honor). 'Prize' in the war sense is current English, and 'brought by sea from Apeira' supplies the capture. An expansion such as 'from the spoils' would add words Butler does not have.

rejected_barriers.quote: Presently
rejected_barriers.reason: Past narrative, where the 'currently' sense cannot apply; the reader recovered it with high confidence. Butler's word, kept as the other Books keep it (e.g. 4.8, 4.23, 5.31, 10.9, 10.41). See recurring.

rejected_barriers.quote: father stranger
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's rendering of xeine pater, a recorded Butlerism kept in both Books (Book 8 continuity §6). Decoded correctly here, at 7.5 and at 8.35.

rejected_barriers.quote: palisade
rejected_barriers.reason: Concrete object in current English; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: a thick cloud of darkness
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's (Homer's) image for Athena's concealing mist; the reader rightly took it as the mist of ¶1.

rejected_barriers.quote: carry his point
rejected_barriers.reason: Current idiom (to win one's case); decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: she comes of the same family as her husband Alcinous
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's statement. ¶6 supplies the niece relationship, as Homer does, and the reader worked it out. Writing 'niece' would add.

rejected_barriers.quote: who was father to Nausithous by Periboea
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Father to X by Y' is current, if formal, genealogical English; decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: reigned over the giants, but he ruined his ill-fated people
rejected_barriers.reason: Mythological background that Homer leaves unexplained; not a wording defect. The reader notes it is not needed for the story, so no gloss.

rejected_barriers.quote: while he was still a bridegroom and without a son
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's statement (Greek numphion, newly married). A bridegroom can leave a daughter, and the succession stays implicit, as in Butler. The reader's reading is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: whom Alcinous married, and honors more than any other woman who keeps house beside her husband
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader's reading matches Butler ('honours as no other woman is honoured'). The uncle–niece marriage stays implicit, as in Butler and Homer.

rejected_barriers.quote: when any women are friends of hers she will help their husbands also to settle their disputes
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler word for word, and the reader's reading (she settles quarrels, even men's, for those she favors) is Butler's. The obscurity is the source's (Od. 7.74); saying whose disputes these are would resolve Butler's own ambiguity. This 'friends' is the current sense and is kept (see B07-02).

rejected_barriers.quote: Scheria
rejected_barriers.reason: Place name established in Book 6; identified correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: the home of Erechtheus
rejected_barriers.reason: Mythological reference that Homer leaves unexplained; outside knowledge. The story does not depend on it.

rejected_barriers.quote: cornice
rejected_barriers.reason: Current architectural term; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: lintel
rejected_barriers.reason: Current architectural term; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: the hook of the door
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's concrete object (Greek korone, a curved door-handle). The reader's 'handle or ring' is right; the exact fitting is uncertain in the source itself.

rejected_barriers.quote: so they were immortal and could never grow old
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's wonder: divine workmanship makes the metal dogs ageless. The reader's reading is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: here and there from one end to the other
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader decoded it ('on both sides'), and 'all along the wall ... from one end to the other' fixes the arrangement. The natural repairs ('on either side', 'on both sides') would echo Butler's own 'On either side', which opens this paragraph for the mastiffs (collision rule). The stakes are small.

rejected_barriers.quote: There are fifty maidservants in the house
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's present-tense description is kept deliberately (Book 7 continuity §5, B07-P010/P011 = p9/p10). The reader recognized the shift.

rejected_barriers.quote: their shuttles go backward and forward like the fluttering of aspen leaves
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's simile, concrete; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: the linen is so closely woven that it sheds oil
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Sheds oil' faithfully modernizes Butler's 'will turn oil', and the reader's reading (oil runs off) is Butler's. Why oil is on the linen is the source's own obscurity (Od. 7.107).

rejected_barriers.quote: Pear grows on pear, apple on apple, and fig on fig
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's image; decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: the one turned in ducts throughout the whole garden
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Ducts' (channels) is current English; the reader took them as irrigation channels.

rejected_barriers.quote: making their drink offerings to Hermes
rejected_barriers.reason: Custom, not wording. 'Drink offering' is the standard English term and the edition holds it steady; explaining the rite would add.

rejected_barriers.quote: laid his hands on the knees of the queen
rejected_barriers.reason: Suppliant gesture, correctly read. Homer does not explain the custom either.

rejected_barriers.quote: and all the honors the state has conferred on them
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's blessing, made its own sentence by the reviewed B07-P013 decision (= p12, continuity §5); decoded. The switch from 'you' to 'them' is Butler's.

rejected_barriers.quote: sat down on the hearth among the ashes
rejected_barriers.reason: Custom, correctly read.

rejected_barriers.quote: the old hero Echeneus
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's standard rendering of heros; decoded (a nobleman).

rejected_barriers.quote: it is not creditable to you
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Creditable' is current English; decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: well-disposed suppliants
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Suppliant' is the standard English term and recurs through the poem; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: golden ewer
rejected_barriers.reason: Concrete object; decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: An upper servant
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's term (Greek tamie; also at 8.41); decoded (a senior servant).

rejected_barriers.quote: handed it round after giving every man his drink offering
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader's reading (a first splash into each cup for the offering, then wine to drink) is exactly the sense (Od. 7.183). The same Butler formula stands verbatim in accepted Book 3 (3.26), so the edition holds it. Any clearer version would have to add the ritual detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: Aldermen and town councilors
rejected_barriers.reason: Recorded keep: Book 7 continuity §5 at B07-P018 (= p17), on the accepted 6.4 precedent, and Book 8 continuity §6 (Butlerism class). Decoded. See recurring.

rejected_barriers.quote: the question of his escort
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's steady word for pompe (conveyance home), defined by the same sentence ('send him back ... to his own country'). Decoded every time. See recurring.

rejected_barriers.quote: But in that case the gods are departing from their usual practice
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's logic, made explicit by the next sentence. With B07-04 its ground (the gods appear openly) is clear as well.

rejected_barriers.quote: as near of kin to the gods as the Cyclopes and the savage giants are
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's reference; outside knowledge. Not a wording defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: let me have my supper in spite of sorrow
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer has him ask to eat while he is already eating (Od. 7.215); the reader's reading is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: my bondservants
rejected_barriers.reason: Accepted rendering (4.54 = B04-P055; Book 7 continuity §3); decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: in the gallery
rejected_barriers.reason: GLOSSARY Book 1 row (Butler's 'cloister' → 'the gallery'), held steady across Books.

rejected_barriers.quote: Did you not say you had come here from beyond the sea?
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's question (Od. 7.239); the reader read the probing correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: called ‘the Ogygian.’
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's form with its nested quotation, preserved deliberately (continuity §4); decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: I stuck to the keel
rejected_barriers.reason: Concrete; decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: of her own free will, either because Zeus had told her she must
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's wording; the tension is his, and the reader read it correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Poseidon would let me go no further
rejected_barriers.reason: Poseidon's hostility is established in earlier Books (assignment note); not a defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: Sick and sorry as I was
rejected_barriers.reason: 'Sorry' = wretched is still current ('a sorry state'); decoded with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: I have told you the whole truth
rejected_barriers.reason: The withheld name is Homer's design (it is revealed in Book 9); not a defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: I thought you might perhaps be displeased if you saw me
rejected_barriers.reason: His tactful cover for Nausicaa depends on Book 6 (assignment note); not a wording defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: even if it is a long way further off than Euboea
rejected_barriers.reason: Place name; the sentence says what matters (it is the furthest place). Kept without a gloss under the 2026-09-23 screening ruling that keeps the Euboea anecdote.

rejected_barriers.quote: When my people took yellow-haired Rhadamanthus to see Tityus the son of Gaia
rejected_barriers.reason: Mythological reference; outside knowledge. The point (a very long voyage done in a day) comes through, as the reader says. Kept under the 2026-09-23 ruling.

rejected_barriers.quote: those of them who saw it told me it is the furthest place of any
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader's reading (it = Euboea) is right, and 'furthest place' rules out Tityus and the voyage. Rhadamanthus's destination is Euboea anyway, so no wrong reading is available. Kept under the 2026-09-23 ruling on this anecdote; if the lead reopens it, 'saw it' → 'saw Euboea' is the one-word option.

rejected_barriers.quote: good red rugs
rejected_barriers.reason: Concrete (Greek rhegea, thick coverings laid on the bed). 'Make it with ... rugs, and ... coverlets on the top of them' decodes it, and the reader read it correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: woolen cloaks for Odysseus to wear
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's detail (cloaks to wrap himself in); decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: a room over the echoing gateway
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's wording for the gatehouse room of ¶27; decoded.

reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.reader_said: He wishes the guests long and happy lives and that they may pass their wealth and public honors on to their children, since he has suffered a long time far from his own people.
reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.butler: to help me home to my own country as soon as possible; for I have been long in trouble and away from my friends.
reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.why_text_is_clear: The reader's own first sentence reports the plea correctly ('humbly begs ... to help him get home to his own country quickly'). A speech-final 'For I have been long in trouble…' reads naturally as the reason for the whole plea, and nothing in the blessing invites a causal link to his suffering, so the 'since' is a paraphrase slip. It is recorded because the reviewed restructure (continuity §5, B07-P013 = p12) moves the blessing between Butler's 'as soon as possible' and its 'for' clause. The only repair would be a further reordering against that decision, so none is proposed.

recurring.item: friends in Butler's kin sense (Greek philoi, one's own people)
recurring.rendering: loved ones (B07-02, B07-03). The current sense stays at 7.7 ('friends of hers'), 8.6, 8.15 (twice), 8.16, 8.36 and 8.49. The same kin sense occurs outside this assignment at 4.39, 5.3, 5.8 and 9.40; the lead may wish to align them.

recurring.item: escort / escorts / escorted (Butler's steady word for pompe, conveyance home by ship)
recurring.rendering: No change. Context defines it at first use (7.17), the reader decoded every instance, and the edition already uses it at 6.22.
No change. Every instance is past narrative, where 'currently' cannot apply; the other Books keep it (4.8, 4.23, 5.31, 10.9, 10.41).
No change. A recorded Butlerism (Book 8 continuity §6), decoded each time.
No change. Recorded keep (Book 7 continuity §5; accepted 6.4; Book 8 continuity §6).

Of a man's build, 'stouter' → 'sturdier' (B08-01). 'Good stout clothing' is kept, because there 'stout' = strong is current; record the split as one by referent. The same Butler phrase 'taller and stouter' recurs at 24.23, outside this assignment.

summary: Book 7 is now broadly comprehensible: the reader's paraphrase is right in all 29 paragraphs, and almost all of the 61 barriers (49 pause, 11 unsure, 1 misread) fall on references carried over from Books 1–6 or left unexplained by Homer, on Homeric custom (supplication, drink offerings), or on the edition's recorded keeps (father stranger, aldermen, gallery, bondservants). Three failures are caused by the text, each in a word or two: Butler's kin sense of 'friends' (7.7, 7.12), the reader's one misread; the pronoun in 'lay with his daughter' (7.6), which parses by default as Poseidon's own daughter; and the idiom 'made themselves perfectly clear' (7.17), which turns the gods' visible appearances, the ground of Alcinous's argument, into clear speech. Four recommended repairs (B07-01 to B07-04) cover them; none is blocking, and every other barrier is ruled on individually. Paragraph numbers here are the 0-based p of the pairs files; continuity and GLOSSARY IDs (B0N-Pnnn) are 1-based.
